contributions.headingText: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) associated with chronic inflammation is an EBV-associated mature B-cell neoplasm occurring in the context of longstanding chronic inflammation, usually in confined anatomical sites.
9680/3 Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma associated with chronic inflammation
2A81.7 Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma associated with chronic inflammation

The commonest site of involvement is the pleural cavity (pyothorax-associated lymphoma [PAL]). Lymphoma occurring in other sites (e.g. bone, joint, and periarticular soft tissue) is not discussed in this section {9422983; 15897752}. Fibrin-associated DLBCL was previously considered a subtype of DLBCL associated with chronic inflammation, but it is now considered a separate, distinct entity (see section Cardiac fibrin-associated diffuse large B-cell lymphoma).

In PAL, there is direct invasion of adjacent structures, but the tumour is often confined to the thoracic cavity at the time of diagnosis, with about 70% of patients presenting with clinical stage I/II disease {16330929; 12377970}.

PAL is the prototypical form, developing in the pleural cavity of patients with longstanding pyothorax. Patients present with chest pain, back pain, fever, or tumorous swelling in the chest wall, or with respiratory symptoms such as productive cough, haemoptysis, or dyspnoea. The serum LDH level is commonly elevated {12377970; 12023576}.

Imaging

Radiological examination reveals a tumour mass in the pleura (80%), pleura and lung (10%), and lung near the pleura (7%).

PAL develops in patients with a 20- to 64-year (median: 37-year) history of pyothorax resulting from artificial pneumothorax for treatment of pulmonary or pleural tuberculosis {16330929; 2681886; 12377970; 12023576; 17043091}. Patient age at diagnosis ranges from the fifth to eighth decade of life, with a median age of 65–70 years {12377970; 17043091}. The M:F ratio is 12:3, versus near equality for chronic pyothorax, suggesting that men are more susceptible to this type of lymphoma {2681886; 12377970}. Although most cases of PAL have been reported in Japan, this lymphoma has also been described in Europe {12023576; 9426333}.

Artificial pneumothorax, used in the past as a form of surgical therapy for pulmonary tuberculosis, is the most significant risk factor for development of PAL among chronic pyothorax patients {8449828; 9515788}. Rare examples arise in the setting of posttraumatic empyema {25968626}. PAL is strongly associated with EBV, with expression of EBNA2 and/or LMP1 together with EBNA1 {8552574; 14556658; 9515788; 8238246}, i.e. usually type III EBV latency {16385574; 12023576}. Chronic inflammation at the local site probably plays a role in the proliferation of EBV-transformed B cells by enabling them to escape from the host immune surveillance through production of IL-10 (an immunosuppressive cytokine) and by providing autocrine to paracrine growth via IL-6 and IL-6R {9006350; 8765317}. Secretion of CCL17 and CCL22 (chemokines that attract CCR4-expressing regulatory T cells) may play a role in immune evasion in PAL {30953706}.

IG genes are clonally rearranged and hypermutated but lack ongoing mutations {12065872; 18079737}. TP53 mutations occur in about 70% of cases, usually involving dipyrimidine sites, which are known to be susceptible to mutagenesis induced by ionizing radiation {9515788}. MYC gene amplification is common {11493333}, and TNFAIP3 (A20) is deleted in a proportion of cases {23418597}. Cytogenetic studies show complex karyotypes with numerous numerical and structural abnormalities {14556658}. The gene expression profile of PAL is distinct from that of nodal DLBCL {15504251}. One of the most differentially expressed genes is IFI27, which is known to be induced in B lymphocytes by stimulation of interferon-α, in keeping with the role of chronic inflammation in this condition. Downregulation of HLA class I expression, which is essential for efficient induction of host cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs), and mutations of CTL epitopes in EBNA3B, an immunodominant antigen for CTL responses, might also contribute to escape of PAL cells from host CTLs {11058881; 10417757}.
The fleshy tumour mass is > 100 mm in more than half of the cases.

The morphological features are the same as those of DLBCL-NOS. Most cases show centroblastic/immunoblastic morphology, with round nuclei and large single or multiple nucleoli. Massive necrosis and angiocentric growth may be present.

Immunohistochemistry

Most cases express CD20 and CD79a. However, a proportion of cases may show plasmacytic differentiation, with loss of CD20 and/or CD79a and expression of IRF4 (MUM1) and CD138. The lymphoma exhibits an activated B-cell / non–germinal-centre B-cell phenotype. CD30 can be expressed. Occasional cases may express in addition one or more T-cell markers (CD2, CD3, CD4, and/or CD7), causing problems in lineage assignment {9422983; 12377970; 12023576; 12769353}.

In situ hybridization for EBV-encoded small RNA (EBER) shows positive labelling of the lymphoma cells. Type III EBV latency is characteristic (LMP1+, EBNA2+) {12023576; 18801089}. HHV8 is negative.

Differential diagnosis

PAL is distinguished from primary effusion lymphoma in that a solid tumour mass is formed, the lymphoma cells often express B-lineage markers, and HHV8 is negative.
EBER may be helpful, as described above.

Essential:

  • Mass-forming tumour involving the pleura
  • Large cell lymphoma with expression of B-lineage markers
  • EBV positivity
  • History of longstanding chronic inflammation

DLBCL associated with chronic inflammation is an aggressive lymphoma. For PAL patients, the 5-year overall survival rate is 20–35% {12377970; 17043091}. For patients achieving complete remission with chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy, the 5-year survival rate is 50% {12377970}. Complete tumour resection (pleuropneumonectomy with or without resection of adjacent involved tissues) or chemotherapy plus rituximab has been reported to give good results {8666866; 31852157}. Poor performance status; high serum levels of LDH, alanine transaminase, or urea; and high clinical stage are unfavourable prognostic factors {1805046; 17043091}.
